title: One-dimensional piecewise-affine reachability
formal: Is there a deterministic Turing machine that always halts and decides, given a one-dimensional rational piecewise-affine map \(f:[0,1]\to[0,1]\) and rational points \(s,t\in[0,1]\), whether \[\exists n\in\mathbb N,\qquad f^n(s)=t?\] The map is specified by finitely many rational linear guards and one rational affine expression on each guard, as defined below. The number of pieces is part of the input and is not bounded by a fixed constant. The question is exact point reachability after finitely many iterations, including zero iterations.

source_formulation.text: Yet, the decidability of the general one-dimensional reachability problem for PAMs remains open, even for maps defined with two pieces.
source_formulation.caption: Complete selected source sentence; PDF p. 2

why: This is an elementary finite description of potentially complicated discrete dynamics: one rational number evolves by affine updates selected through interval tests. Exact reachability is the basic question behind checking whether such an iteration ever attains a specified state. A resolution would locate a decidability boundary between the tractable affine orbit problem and the already undecidable higher-dimensional piecewise-affine setting.
status_note: Source-open in the MFCS paper published 20 August 2025, which explicitly includes the unresolved two-piece subcase. The checked March 2023 injective theorem and the MFCS Bellman-operator results impose additional restrictions. A bounded later-work search on 16 September 2026 found no matching resolution. This is a dated literature-status assessment, not independent proof that no later solution exists or verification of all cited proofs.

progress.text: Koiran, Cosnard and Garzon establish undecidability of piecewise-affine reachability already in dimension two. The checked MFCS introduction contrasts this with the unresolved dimension-one problem.

The revised injective-maps paper proves Theorem 1.1: exact reachability is decidable for injective one-dimensional maps with two half-open interval pieces. The general two-piece case remains outside that theorem.
The MFCS paper explicitly retains general one-dimensional reachability as open, even for two pieces. Its positive Bellman-operator theorems impose a different structural restriction.

The exact domain, rational point target and guard conventions were checked along with the injective subclass theorem. A bounded search located no matching later resolution for arbitrary one-dimensional rational piecewise-affine maps.

importance.reason: A longstanding and basic reachability problem at the boundary between elementary numerical dynamics and undecidable systems. Its unresolved two-piece subcase, exact rational arithmetic and connections to verification make the general one-dimensional problem broadly significant.
importance.basis: Individual assessment from the MFCS 2025 open statement and the 2023 injective two-piece result.

sentences: A one-dimensional rational piecewise-affine map repeatedly updates one number using the affine expression selected by its interval guards.
The question asks whether exact reachability of a rational target from a rational starting point is decidable for every finite description.
The number of pieces is unrestricted, all boundary choices are explicit, and any finite number of iterations including zero is allowed.
Injective two-piece maps and certain Bellman operators admit decision procedures, but the checked source retains the general question as open.
A resolution would locate a basic boundary between finite descriptions of numerical dynamics and algorithmic reachability analysis.

definitions: The domain is the closed real unit interval \([0,1]=\{x\in\mathbb R:0\le x\le1\}\), following the source's unit-cube convention in dimension one. An input specifies an integer \(k\ge1\). For each \(i\le k\), a piece \(P_i\subseteq[0,1]\) is defined by a finite conjunction of inequalities \(\alpha x<\beta\) or \(\alpha x\le\beta\), with \(\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb Q\), and its affine expression is \(a_i x+b_i\), with \(a_i,b_i\in\mathbb Q\). Negative or zero slopes are allowed. The input must satisfy \[\bigcup_{i=1}^{k}P_i=[0,1],\qquad a_i x+b_i=a_jx+b_j\quad(x\in P_i\cap P_j),\qquad 0\le a_ix+b_i\le1\quad(x\in P_i).\] These conditions make \(f(x)=a_ix+b_i\) for \(x\in P_i\) a total single-valued self-map. Pieces are intervals, possibly empty or singletons; strict versus non-strict inequalities specify endpoint ownership exactly. When pieces overlap their formulas must agree, rather than using an implicit priority between guards. The map need not be continuous, injective, monotone or contractive. No Bellman-operator promise is imposed. Each rational is encoded by a signed binary numerator and a positive binary denominator, and the finite lists of guards and coefficients use explicit delimiters. The numbers \(s\) and \(t\) are encoded the same way. All input validity conditions are finite rational linear conditions; invalid descriptions may be rejected. Define \(f^0(s)=s\) and \(f^{n+1}(s)=f(f^n(s))\), with \(\mathbb N=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}\). Since the initial point and all affine coefficients are rational, every orbit point is rational, even though the map is defined on the real interval. Equality with \(t\) is exact rational equality. One uniform machine must answer all finite inputs, regardless of coefficient bit lengths and piece count, with no oracle, random error or prescribed time bound. The number of iterations is existentially quantified and has no input-supplied upper bound.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of decidability or undecidability for the defined finite input language. An affirmative proof must provide a uniform terminating algorithm, correct for both reachable and unreachable rational targets. A negative proof must establish that no total computable decider exists. Decidability for two pieces or another restricted class is partial unless extended to arbitrary finite piece counts; undecidability within such a subclass would suffice for a negative answer. Approaching the target arbitrarily closely, reaching an interval around it, bounded-horizon simulation or a theorem for two-dimensional maps does not settle the displayed exact one-dimensional question.

context_blocks.text: With one piece, every iteration uses the same affine formula. With several pieces, the current value determines which update is applied next. The choice is deterministic, but the itinerary through the pieces may encode a long and complicated pattern. Rational coefficients do not make the state space finite: repeated division can produce infinitely many different denominators.

The target is a single rational point. For example, \(f(x)=x/2\) started at \(s=1\) converges to zero but never reaches \(t=0\) in finitely many iterations. Consequently a limiting value, an approximate numerical trajectory and exact reachability answer different questions. The zero-iteration convention means that every instance with \(s=t\) is immediately a yes-instance.

The source describes the general one-dimensional question and emphasizes that even two pieces remain unresolved. The card retains the full general target. A positive result limited to two pieces would be important progress without deciding all finite piece counts; a negative result for two pieces would also prove the general problem undecidable.

Ghahremani, Kelmendi and Ouaknine prove decidability when a two-piece map is injective, meaning distinct inputs have distinct images. Their precise convention uses a half-open unit interval partitioned into two half-open intervals. This is a restricted positive theorem; neither injectivity nor that endpoint convention is silently imposed on the present general closed-domain statement.

The MFCS source studies a different restriction: Bellman operators describing updates of reachability probabilities in finite Markov decision processes. Under its stated absence-of-end-components assumption, it obtains several arbitrary-dimensional decision results and a complete two-dimensional result for that subclass. These operators satisfy structural constraints absent from an arbitrary piecewise-affine map, so those theorems do not resolve the open one-dimensional class here.

A finite list of guards must define one function, including all boundary points. The source permits pieces described by strict and non-strict linear inequalities and requires the same function on overlaps. Recording those conventions prevents a rounding rule or an unstated branch priority from changing an orbit exactly at a breakpoint.
